We had to find a pose that read with definition and appeal. Straight Ahead Action and Pose to Pose There are two main approaches to animation. The first is known as Straight Ahead Action because the anima- tor literally works straight ahead from his first drawing in the scene. He simply takes off, doing one drawing after the Other, getting new ideas as he along_ until he reaches the end of the scene. He knows the Story pint Of the scene and the business that is to be included. but he has little plan of how it Will all be done at the time he starts. Both the drawings and the action have a fresh. slightly zany look, as the animator keeps the whole prcxess very creative. The second is called pose to Pose. Here, the anima- tor plans his action, figures out just which drawings Will needed to animate the business, makes the drawings, relating them to each Other in si7C and action. and gives the scene to his assistant to draw the tweens. Acting and Emotions "In Our animation we must show not only 'he actions or reactions of a character, but we must picture also with the action . . . the feeling Of those Stokowski recognized Walt•s truly unique tal- ent when he commented. • 'Walt had the imagination, insight, humor. and sense of design to enter into the feeling of life of any man. animal, Cree. or stone and make us feel with him- "1 From the very txginning, it was obvious that these feelings of the characters would the heart and soul of the Disney Pictures. The stories, which at first had txen told through bits of business incidents, were told more and more through the reactions of the characters to those incidents. The inci- dents thernselves remained vital to the story, but how the characters felt about What was happening more important. In every art form it is the emotional content that makes the difference mere technical skill and true art. The poet. sculptor. dancer, painter, Singer, actor—all eventually can proficient in their crafts. achieving dazzling mechanical perfection, but their work Will empty and meaningless unless the Frsonal perceptions of the artist are Communicated as well. This thought was stated most simply by one Studio artist when he noted that many of the Young men 'Scould animate but that isn•t What makes you laugh and that isn't What makes the tears Walt Disney In the animated film there is actually a double pten- tial for this tyF of personal expression; first. in the emotions of the characters in the film that arouse addi- tional respnses in the audience, and, second, in the artistry Of the work itself. It Will show in the writing and the choice of the material, in the design and pre• sentation, the staging. the Picture-making, the voice talents, the color, the music—and especially in the animation. There are the individual drawings with their elusive sensation Of life, and there are the relation- of all the drawings in movement and time. In this book we have outlined the basic skills that must mastered if strong. Clear communication is to achieved. We also have pointed out many examples of fine animation that txcarne memorable txcause of feelings the artist had atx)ut the character and the situa- tion. There was more than just frowning in anger, more (han a single expression. or even one lone con- vincing scene. There was real drama with the full range of emotions. its Ilituted repertoire of grimaces over alid over. Great scenes were never that way. Katharine Ommanney. in her book On for students, has defined the rules and the exercises that are the steps for the tx•ginner. 2 She asks the Frforrner to consider these questions as he tries to «'tnmunicate with an audience: Are the characters interesting. lifelike. and vivid? They sound so simple, written this way. and are easy to pin up on one's desk—but so difficult to achieve. The demands were quite simple in the Carly films. limited mainly to gestures of annoyance that tried to ••anger•• and a kind of fright that wished it could "fear." Gradually a kind of formula developed for making • 'pathos" the prime ingredient in a film. such as The Ugly Duckling: an apFaling little character Wants very much to achieve something and fails in a way that hurts him: the Other characters ridicule him: he tries again. fails again; the audience feels the hurt and Starts to pull for the little guy: when he finally succeeds in a unique and heartwarming way, everyone feels like cheering. It is an Old formula and the acting choices are ele. mental. As long as the central figure is sincere, his actions can broad and touched with humor without upsetting the pathos. The ugly duckling•s mournful Cry of rejection was a ludicrous honk. which only the awareness in the audience that this little outcast did, indeed. have a real problem. Laugh- ter and sympathy were combined in a way that of. fered a high potential for entertainment and for sonality development. but there were no great demands in acting. \nalysis of Donald Duck Character and Personality Donald has developed into One Of the most interesting screen comics. The audi- ence always likes him. provided he plays true to his Own character. His best fea- tures are his ccxky, show-off, tx»astful at- titude that turns to anger as soon as he is crossed; his typical angry gestures with which the audience is familiar, esrxcially his fighting pose and his Exculiar quack- ing voice and threats when angry. The Duck gets a big kick out of impos- ing on Other or annoying them; but immediately Ic»es his temrxr when the tables are turned. In other words, he can "dish it out" but he can't ' •take it". The Duck takes himself very seriously. He has a high opinion Of himself, and as as anything wrong, he immecii- ately wants to fight. When he is pleased with himself, or happy about something he has done, we show his nervous charac- ter by wiggling his tail. I don't think it wise to use the tail wiggle when he is angry. He has a very suspiciOus nature; is quick-tempered but is just dumb enough to trapFd repeatedly into losing his temper. However. he is not as dumb as Pluto or the Goof. Donald cannot be fun- ny if the situation does not fit his peculiar mannensms. General Construction A. Donald is drawn as Fred Moore draws Mickey. He is one piece rather than two parts•, has a body; is short, squatty, and is drawn to show weight in the body. Keep as much weight in him as IX)ssible, that is, feel that he is hugging the ground. To at- tain the tx•st results, one leg is bent and the Other kept straight. The straight leg is as short as keeping the bulky mass down close to the ground. Keeping the leg up into the and showing a sag under- neath Will help to get a feeling of weight. B. Size of head and neck C. D. The size Of the head is to be half the size of the lower part Of the tN)dy, and is kept round. To show anger, give a ruftled effect on the head; but Otherwise keep the head smooth. The neck is thicker at the head than it is at the body end and is to be kept weighty, but not long. Eyes. Bill. and Cheeks The most important thing about ald is his expressions. A lot can done in this connectiOn with the eyes and the eyebrows. We also find that the hat and the position Of the bill help the expression of the eyes. The eyebrows are used in the Same way that pluto's eyebrows are used. they protrude the top circle Of the head. The are not round as in previ- ous pictures. They are more oval in shaF and are kept to the side of the head- In this way more black can be used in the eyes for the expressions. When the eyes are closed, we break up the circle and animate it into a round- The eyes are kept Wide apart to give better expresion and on a 3/4 View the eye On the side is Iost. The top part of the bill fits into the center Of the head- Instead Of there txing a straight line from the top Of the head down to the end Of the bill, the corner Of the bill curves into the inside of the head when he smiles or is happy; when Donald frowns or is angry, it protrudes on the outside Of the circle of the head with a down-in- the-mouth feeling. We use cheeks on Donald only when we indicate chewing Or blowing. Legs and Feet The legs are suppOsed to short and squatty and the feet kept large to give more Of a comedy The feet have three toes and they are neither pointed nor long, but a happy medium between the tw0.
